title: Measurement, Time & Money
blurb: Centimetres and metres, grams and kilograms, litres and millilitres, reading the clock to the quarter hour, the calendar, and counting togrog and making change.

lessons.title: Length: cm and m
lessons.concreteComparison: Put one finger on a single centimetre mark of your school ruler and step it along the wall of a ger — you would have to step it a hundred times to cross one metre stick's worth of felt. That is the whole deal between the two length units: one metre TRADES for exactly $100$ centimetres, the way one big note trades for a fixed stack of small ones. Know the trade, then count.
lessons.objective: Measure lengths with a ruler (even when the object does not start at the $0$ mark), choose the sensible unit — centimetres for small things, metres for big ones — and convert between metres and centimetres both ways.
concept: **One metre trades for 100 centimetres.** The centimetre is the small unit (about a fingernail's width); the metre is the big one (a giant step). The trade is fixed: $1$ m $= 100$ cm, so $3$ m $= 3 \times 100 = 300$ cm.

**A ruler measures from mark to mark.** If the object starts at $0$, read its end. If it starts elsewhere, subtract the start mark from the end mark: from the $2$ to the $9$ is $7$ cm, because $7 + 2 = 9$.
**Compare in ONE unit.** Is $2$ m longer than $180$ cm? Bare numbers lie ($180 > 2$). Trade first: $2$ m $= 200$ cm, and $200 > 180$ — the metres win. Same unit, then compare.
lessons.keyIdea: One metre trades for exactly 100 centimetres. Measure from mark to mark, pick cm for small things and m for big ones, and never compare lengths until both wear the same unit.

facts.title: The length trade
facts.explanation: The fixed trade: every metre is worth one hundred centimetres.

facts.title: Mark to mark
facts.explanation: An object lying from the 2 cm mark to the 9 cm mark is 7 cm long — subtract the marks, and add back to check.

workedExamples.statement: A table is $2$ m long and a bench is $180$ cm long. Which is longer?
workedExamples.note: Trade into one unit before comparing.
workedExamples.solution: Trade the metres: $2$ m $= 2 \times 100 = 200$ cm. Now both wear centimetres: $200 > 180$, so the table is longer — by $20$ cm, since $180 + 20 = 200$ ✓.

workedExamples.statement: A stick lies along a ruler from the $2$ cm mark to the $9$ cm mark. How long is the stick?
workedExamples.note: Not starting at 0 — subtract the marks.
workedExamples.solution: Mark to mark: $9 - 2 = 7$ cm. Add back to check: $7 + 2 = 9$ ✓. The stick is $7$ cm long.

commonMistakes.text: Trading a metre for 10 centimetres — writing 3 m = 30 cm.
commonMistakes.correction: The trade is 100 per metre, not 10: 3 m = 300 cm. Say the trade out loud before multiplying.

commonMistakes.text: Comparing 2 m with 180 cm by the bare numbers and deciding 180 wins.
commonMistakes.correction: Numbers in different units cannot be compared. Trade first: 2 m = 200 cm, and 200 > 180.

tryIt.statement: Convert $6$ m to centimetres, and $900$ cm to metres.
tryIt.solution: Big to small multiplies the trade: $6 \times 100 = 600$ cm. Small to big divides it: $900 \div 100 = 9$ m.

tryIt.statement: A ger door is about $2$ m tall. Could it be $2$ cm instead? Explain with the trade.
tryIt.solution: No — $2$ m $= 200$ cm, taller than you. $2$ cm is about the width of two fingernails: $200 > 2$, a door of $2$ cm would not let a cat through.

steps.title: The 100-trade, and the ruler
beats: Two length units, one fixed trade: $1$ metre $= 100$ centimetres. A centimetre is a fingernail's width; a metre is a giant step — and every metre is worth exactly $100$ of the small ones.
The ruler below shows a pencil measured from the $0$ mark: its tip reaches $7$, so it is $7$ cm long. Starting at $0$ lets the end mark do all the work.
The through-line of this whole topic: KNOW THE TRADE. Every unit here swaps for a fixed count of smaller ones — length starts us off with $100$ cm per metre.

steps.title: Trading and measuring
steps.intro: Multiply the trade going big-to-small; subtract marks on the ruler.

examples.prompt: Convert $3$ m to centimetres.
steps: The trade: each metre is worth $100$ cm.

examples.prompt: A stick lies from the $2$ cm mark to the $9$ cm mark. Its length?
steps: The stick does not start at $0$ — subtract the marks: $9 - 2 = 7$ cm.

steps.title: Trade and read
steps.intro: Say the trade first; subtract marks second.

problems.prompt: $5$ m in centimetres is:
problems.explanation: The trade is $100$ per metre: $5 \times 100 = 500$ cm. Writing $50$ trades only $10$ per metre, and $105$ adds instead of trading.

problems.prompt: A crayon lies from the $4$ cm mark to the $12$ cm mark. It is:
problems.explanation: Subtract the marks: $12 - 4 = 8$ cm, and $8 + 4 = 12$ ✓. Reading $12$ forgets the crayon started at $4$; adding the marks measures nothing at all.

problems.prompt: $700$ cm in metres is:
problems.explanation: Small to big divides the trade: $700 \div 100 = 7$ m, and $7 \times 100 = 700$ ✓. $70$ divides by $10$ instead of $100$.

steps.title: The trade
steps.prompt: How many centimetres are in $4$ metres?
steps.explanation: Each metre trades for $100$ cm: $4 \times 100 = 400$. The wrong answers trade at $10$, at $1$, and at $250$ — but the length trade never changes: $100$ per metre.

steps.title: Your body carries rulers
steps.body: Stretch both arms out wide: for most people, fingertip to fingertip is about the same as their own height — your body is a rough measuring tape you always carry. Rough is the key word: real rulers win because they trade in exact centimetres, $100$ to every metre, the same for everybody.

steps.title: Sensible units, honest comparisons
beats: Pick the unit that fits the job: CENTIMETRES for small things (a pencil, a book, your hand), METRES for big ones (a ger, a classroom, a rope for the horses). The line below is the whole metre laid out in centimetres — $100$ small steps.
To compare lengths in DIFFERENT units, trade first: $3$ m of rope against $280$ cm of rope is really $300$ cm against $280$ cm — the metres win by $20$.
Never compare bare numbers across units. $180 > 2$ says nothing about $180$ cm and $2$ m; only after the trade ($200$ cm) does the comparison become honest.

steps.title: Same unit, then compare
steps.intro: Trade everything into centimetres; then the bigger number wins.

examples.prompt: Which is longer: $3$ m of rope, or $280$ cm of rope?
steps: $300 > 280$ — the $3$ m rope is longer by $20$ cm, since $280 + 20 = 300$ ✓.

examples.prompt: A classroom is $8$ m long. How many centimetres is that, and why do we say $8$ m rather than $800$ cm?
steps: Both are true — but $8$ is a friendlier count than $800$, so for big things the big unit is the sensible choice.

steps.title: Pick the unit, win the comparison
steps.intro: Small things take cm; big things take m; comparisons take ONE unit.

problems.prompt: The sensible unit for a toothbrush's length is:
problems.explanation: A toothbrush is about $15$ cm — much less than a whole metre, since $15 < 100$. Metres would make it a strange fraction, and kilograms measure mass, not length.

problems.prompt: Which is shorter: $190$ cm or $2$ m?
problems.explanation: Trade: $2$ m $= 200$ cm. Then $190 < 200$, so the $190$ cm length is shorter. Comparing $190$ against the bare $2$ is the trap.

problems.prompt: A rope measures $400$ cm. In metres that is:
problems.explanation: Divide by the trade: $400 \div 100 = 4$ m, and $4 \times 100 = 400$ ✓. $40$ m would be a rope as long as five classrooms.

steps.title: Does the carpet fit?
steps.prompt: Baatar's ger is $5$ m across. A carpet is $480$ cm wide. Does the carpet fit?
options: yes — $480$ cm is less than $500$ cm
steps.explanation: Trade the ger's width: $5$ m $= 500$ cm. Then $480 < 500$ — the carpet fits with $20$ cm to spare ($480 + 20 = 500$ ✓). Comparing $480$ with the bare $5$ is the different-units trap.

steps.title: What you learned
points: One metre trades for exactly 100 centimetres — the fixed trade.
Big to small multiplies by 100; small to big divides by 100.
On a ruler, measure from mark to mark: subtract the start from the end.
Centimetres for small things, metres for big ones.
Compare lengths only after trading them into ONE unit.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every item below, say the trade out loud first — one metre, one hundred centimetres — and check whether your two lengths wear the same unit before you compare.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Trades both ways, ruler reads, and honest comparisons.

problems.prompt: $9$ m in centimetres is:
problems.explanation: $9 \times 100 = 900$ cm. Trading at $10$ gives the too-small $90$.

problems.prompt: A piece of chalk lies from the $1$ cm mark to the $10$ cm mark. Its length is:
problems.explanation: Subtract the marks: $10 - 1 = 9$ cm, and $9 + 1 = 10$ ✓. Reading the end mark alone ignores where the chalk starts.

problems.prompt: $1\,000$ cm in metres is:
Which is longer: $6$ m or $590$ cm?
A door's height is about:
problems.explanation: A door is a big thing — metres fit. $2$ m $= 200$ cm, taller than you; $2$ cm would not let a mouse through, and $200$ m is taller than any building in the town — about a hundred doors stacked up.

steps.title: You've finished "Length: cm and m"
steps.body: One fixed trade — $100$ centimetres to the metre — plus mark-to-mark measuring and one-unit comparisons. Next: the same game with heavier stakes, where kilograms and litres each trade for a THOUSAND small units.

lessons.title: Mass & Capacity
lessons.concreteComparison: At the market a trader drops a whole kilogram weight on one pan of the balance scale and pours aaruul onto the other, piece by piece, until the pans level out. Each little piece weighs a few grams — and it takes a full $1\,000$ grams of them to balance that one kilogram. Milk plays the same game in a jug: $1\,000$ millilitres fill exactly one litre.
lessons.objective: Use the trades $1$ kg $= 1\,000$ g and $1$ l $= 1\,000$ ml, choose the sensible unit for a mass or a capacity, convert whole numbers both ways, and compare two amounts after trading them into one unit.
concept: **One kilogram trades for 1000 grams.** Grams weigh small things — a letter, an egg, a sweet. Kilograms weigh big ones — a sack of flour, a young goat, you. The trade is fixed: $2$ kg $= 2 \times 1\,000 = 2\,000$ g.
**One litre trades for 1000 millilitres.** Millilitres measure spoonfuls and cups; litres measure jugs, pots and buckets. Same fixed trade, new letters: $3$ l $= 3\,000$ ml.
**Compare in one unit — same rule as length.** Is $2$ kg more than $1\,900$ g? Trade first: $2$ kg $= 2\,000$ g, and $2\,000 > 1\,900$. The bare numbers ($1\,900$ against $2$) would have lied again.
lessons.keyIdea: Kilograms and litres both trade for exactly 1000 of their small units. Grams and millilitres for small amounts, kilograms and litres for big ones — and no comparison until both amounts wear the same unit.

facts.title: The two 1000-trades
facts.explanation: Mass and capacity trade big-for-small at the same fixed rate: one thousand.

facts.title: Mixed amounts
facts.explanation: 2 l 500 ml is 2500 ml — trade the litres, then add the loose millilitres.

workedExamples.statement: Convert $4$ kg to grams, and $5\,000$ g to kilograms.
workedExamples.note: Big to small multiplies the trade; small to big divides it.

workedExamples.statement: A jug holds $2$ l of milk; a bottle holds $1\,500$ ml. Which holds more?

commonMistakes.text: Trading a kilogram for 100 grams — writing 2 kg = 200 g.
commonMistakes.correction: Length trades at 100, but mass and capacity trade at 1000: 2 kg = 2000 g. Each unit has its own fixed rate — say it before you multiply.

commonMistakes.text: Deciding 900 ml is more than 1 l because 900 > 1.
commonMistakes.correction: Different units cannot be compared bare. Trade: 1 l = 1000 ml, and 900 < 1000 — the litre wins.

tryIt.statement: Convert $3$ l to millilitres, and $8\,000$ ml to litres.
A watermelon weighs about $5$ kg. Could it be $5$ g instead?
tryIt.solution: No — $5$ kg $= 5\,000$ g, a proper two-handed carry. $5$ g is lighter than a single sweet: $5 < 5\,000$, a $5$ g watermelon would be a crumb.

steps.title: Grams and kilograms — the 1000-trade
beats: Mass has a small unit and a big one, just like length — but the trade is bigger: $1$ kilogram $= 1\,000$ grams. A gram is a sweet's weight; a kilogram is a full bag of flour.
The scale below shows a melon of $800$ g against the full kilogram mark: it falls $200$ g short, because $800 + 200 = 1\,000$.
The trades so far: metres trade at $100$, kilograms at $1\,000$. Different rates, same game — KNOW THE TRADE, then count.

steps.title: Trading grams and kilograms
steps.intro: Multiply by 1000 going big-to-small; divide coming back.

examples.prompt: Convert $2$ kg to grams.
steps: The trade: each kilogram is worth $1\,000$ g.

examples.prompt: A young goat weighs $9$ kg. How many grams — and is the goat heavier than a $950$ g bag of aaruul?
steps: $9\,000 > 950$ — the goat outweighs the bag many times over.

steps.title: The mass trade
steps.intro: 1000 grams per kilogram — both directions.

problems.prompt: $6$ kg in grams is:
problems.explanation: $6 \times 1\,000 = 6\,000$ g. $600$ trades at length's rate of $100$ — mass trades at $1\,000$.

problems.prompt: $7\,000$ g in kilograms is:
The sensible unit for an apple's mass is:
problems.explanation: An apple weighs about $150$ g — well under one kilogram, since $150 < 1\,000$. Kilograms suit sacks and goats; centimetres measure length, not mass.

steps.title: Trade before you judge
steps.prompt: Which is heavier: $2$ kg of flour, or $1\,900$ g of rice?
options: the rice — $1\,900$ is a bigger number than $2$
steps.explanation: Trade first: $2$ kg $= 2\,000$ g. Then $1\,900 < 2\,000$ — the flour wins by $100$ g ($1\,900 + 100 = 2\,000$ ✓). Comparing $1\,900$ with the bare $2$ is the units trap again.

steps.title: A litre of water weighs a kilogram
steps.body: Pour exactly one litre of water into a bottle and set it on a scale: it weighs almost exactly one kilogram — $1\,000$ ml of water comes to about $1\,000$ g. That is no accident: the units were designed to match, so this lesson's two trades are secretly one.

steps.title: Litres and millilitres
beats: Capacity — how much a container holds — has the same shape of trade: $1$ litre $= 1\,000$ millilitres. A spoon holds about $5$ ml; a milk jug holds a litre or two; a bucket holds many.
The jug below is filled to $750$ ml: past the half-litre mark ($500$ ml), still $250$ short of the full litre, because $750 + 250 = 1\,000$.
Mixed amounts trade in two moves: $2$ l $500$ ml is $2\,000 + 500 = 2\,500$ ml. Trade the litres, then add the loose millilitres.

steps.title: Trading litres and millilitres
steps.intro: Same 1000-trade, new containers.

examples.prompt: Convert $5$ l to millilitres.
steps: The trade: each litre is worth $1\,000$ ml.

examples.prompt: Which holds more: a $1\,200$ ml pot, or a $1$ l bottle — and by how much?
steps: The pot holds more, by $200$ ml.

steps.title: The capacity trade
steps.intro: 1000 millilitres per litre.

problems.prompt: $4$ l in millilitres is:
problems.explanation: $4 \times 1\,000 = 4\,000$ ml — capacity trades at $1\,000$, like mass.

problems.prompt: $9\,000$ ml in litres is:
A bowl of airag holds $300$ ml. Half a litre is:
problems.explanation: Half of $1\,000$ ml is $500$ ml, and $300 < 500$ — the half-litre wins.

steps.title: Mixed amounts
steps.prompt: A teapot holds $2\,500$ ml. In litres and millilitres that is:
steps.explanation: Trade out the full litres: $2 \times 1\,000 = 2\,000$, leaving $500$ loose millilitres — $2\,000 + 500 = 2\,500$ ✓. Writing $2$ l $50$ ml drops a zero from the leftover.

steps.title: What you learned
points: One kilogram trades for 1000 grams; one litre trades for 1000 millilitres.
Grams and millilitres for small amounts; kilograms and litres for big ones.
Big to small multiplies by 1000; small to big divides by 1000.
Mixed amounts: trade the big unit, then add the loose small ones.
Compare only after trading both amounts into ONE unit.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Before every answer below, name the trade in play — one hundred for length, one thousand for mass and capacity — then decide which direction you are trading.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Both 1000-trades, both directions, honest comparisons.

problems.prompt: $8$ kg in grams is:
Which is heavier: $2\,500$ g or $3$ kg?
$6\,000$ ml in litres is:
Each flour bag holds $2$ kg, and there are $3$ bags. The total mass in grams is:
problems.explanation: Count the kilograms first: $3 \times 2 = 6$ kg. Then trade: $6 \times 1\,000 = 6\,000$ g. $3\,000$ g counts only half the bags.

problems.prompt: A spoon holds about:
problems.explanation: A spoonful is tiny next to a litre: $5 < 1\,000$. Five litres is a full bucket, and kilograms measure mass, not how much a spoon holds.

steps.title: You've finished "Mass & Capacity"
steps.body: Two more fixed trades — a thousand grams to the kilogram, a thousand millilitres to the litre — and the same one-unit rule for comparing. Next: a trade that is NOT built from tens at all — the sixty-minute hour.

lessons.title: Reading the Clock
lessons.concreteComparison: The minute hand runs a race track of $60$ little steps, once around every hour. Four flags stand on the track: the start at $12$ (o'clock), the quarter flag at $3$ ($15$ minutes), the halfway flag at $6$ ($30$ minutes), and the three-quarter flag at $9$ ($45$ minutes) — where we stop saying PAST and start saying TO the next hour.
lessons.objective: Read o'clock, half past, quarter past and quarter to on a clock face, say each as minutes past the hour, and use the fact that one hour trades for exactly $60$ minutes.
concept: **One hour trades for 60 minutes.** Not $100$ — sixty. The minute hand's full lap is $60$ minutes; the hour hand meanwhile creeps from one number to the next. Two half-laps make the lap: $30 + 30 = 60$.

**Half past and quarter past are fractions of 60.** Half the lap is $60 \div 2 = 30$ minutes (minute hand at $6$); a quarter lap is $60 \div 4 = 15$ minutes (minute hand at $3$). Half past $7$ means $7$:$30$.

**Quarter to names the NEXT hour.** At $45$ minutes past (minute hand at $9$), three quarters are done — $3 \times 15 = 45$ — and one quarter remains: $45 + 15 = 60$. So $7$:$45$ is called quarter to $8$, not quarter to $7$.
lessons.keyIdea: The hour trades for 60 minutes. O'clock is 0 minutes past, quarter past is 15, half past is 30, and quarter to is 45 — a quarter short of the NEXT hour.

facts.title: The quarter marks
facts.explanation: A quarter of the hour is 15 minutes; half is 30. The clock's flags are fractions of sixty.

facts.title: Quarter to
facts.explanation: At 45 minutes past, one quarter remains — so the time is named TO the next hour.

workedExamples.statement: The minute hand points at $6$ and the hour hand sits halfway between $7$ and $8$. What time is it?
workedExamples.note: Minute hand at 6 = half the lap.
workedExamples.solution: Half the $60$-minute lap is $60 \div 2 = 30$ minutes. The hour hand left $7$ but has not reached $8$: it is half past $7$, written $7$:$30$. Another half-lap reaches $8$ o'clock: $30 + 30 = 60$ ✓.

workedExamples.note: Quarter to means 15 minutes BEFORE the named hour.
workedExamples.solution: A quarter of the hour is $60 \div 4 = 15$ minutes. Quarter to $4$ is $15$ minutes before $4$ o'clock — so the hour showing is still $3$, with $3 \times 15 = 45$ minutes past: $3$:$45$. Check: $45 + 15 = 60$ ✓.

commonMistakes.correction: Quarter TO names the hour coming NEXT: 7:45 is 15 minutes before 8, so it is quarter to 8. The hour digit on the clock lags behind the name.

commonMistakes.text: Treating the hour as 100 minutes — half past as 50 minutes.
commonMistakes.correction: The hour trades for 60 minutes, so half past is 60 divided by 2, which is 30 — the minute hand at the 6, not at some 50-mark.

tryIt.statement: Where does the minute hand point at quarter past $9$, and how is the time written in digits?
tryIt.solution: A quarter lap is $60 \div 4 = 15$ minutes, so the minute hand points at $3$. In digits: $9$:$15$.

tryIt.statement: How many minutes does the minute hand take for one full lap of the clock?
tryIt.solution: Four quarter-laps of $15$ make the lap: $4 \times 15 = 60$ minutes — one hour. Two half-laps agree: $2 \times 30 = 60$ ✓.

steps.title: O'clock and half past
beats: The clock face sketched below shows $3$ o'clock: the twelve hour marks ring the rim, the long minute hand points straight up at $12$ — zero minutes past — and the short hour hand points at $3$. At $3$ o'clock the two hands even make a perfect square corner.
The hour's trade is SIXTY: one full lap of the minute hand is $60$ minutes, and from $12$:$00$ to $3$:$00$ it has made three laps — $3 \times 60 = 180$ minutes.
When the minute hand reaches $6$, it has run HALF its lap: $60 \div 2 = 30$ minutes past. Hour hand between $4$ and $5$ with minute hand at $6$ reads: half past $4$.

steps.title: Reading the easy flags
steps.intro: Minute hand at 12: o'clock. Minute hand at 6: half past.

examples.prompt: The minute hand points at $12$ and the hour hand at $3$. The time?
steps: Minute hand at $12$: zero minutes past — an o'clock time.
Since $12$:$00$ the minute hand has lapped $3$ times: $3 \times 60 = 180$ minutes. It is $3$ o'clock.

examples.prompt: Write "half past $9$" in digits.

steps.title: O'clock and half past
steps.intro: Find the minute hand first; it names the flag.

problems.prompt: The minute hand points at $6$; the hour hand sits between $4$ and $5$. The time is:
problems.explanation: Minute hand at $6$ means $60 \div 2 = 30$ minutes past. The hour hand has LEFT $4$ but not reached $5$ — so the hour is still $4$: half past $4$. Reading the nearer number $5$ is the trap.

problems.prompt: How many minutes pass from $7$:$00$ to half past $7$?
problems.explanation: Half the hour's lap: $60 \div 2 = 30$ minutes.

problems.prompt: One full lap of the minute hand takes:
problems.explanation: The hour trades for sixty: two half-laps of $30$ make it ($2 \times 30 = 60$), and four quarter-laps of $15$ agree ($4 \times 15 = 60$). $100$ is the tens reflex — clocks refuse it.

steps.title: Find the minute hand
steps.prompt: At half past $11$, the minute hand points at:
steps.explanation: Half past means half the lap is run: $60 \div 2 = 30$ minutes, which is the $6$ at the bottom of the face. The hour hand is the one near $11$ — mixing the hands up swaps the whole reading.

steps.title: Why 60 and not 100?
steps.body: The 60-minute hour comes from ancient Babylon, and it survived because $60$ splits so cleanly: by $2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20$ and $30$. So half an hour is a whole $30$, a third is $20$, a quarter is $15$ — no leftovers. A 100-minute hour would make a third of an hour impossible to say in whole minutes.

steps.title: Quarter past and quarter to
beats: The minute track below lays the lap out straight, with all four flags. A quarter of the lap is $60 \div 4 = 15$ minutes: minute hand at $3$, and we say QUARTER PAST — quarter past $6$ is $6$:$15$.
At the $9$, three quarters are done: $3 \times 15 = 45$ minutes past. Only one quarter remains — $45 + 15 = 60$ — so we name the hour that is COMING: quarter to.
Quarter to $8$ is therefore $7$:$45$. The digits keep the old hour; the name looks ahead to the new one. That switch is the only tricky step on the whole track.

steps.title: The quarter flags
steps.intro: 15 past: quarter past. 45 past: quarter TO the next hour.

examples.prompt: Write "quarter past $6$" in digits.
Write "quarter to $8$" in digits.
steps: Quarter to $8$ is $15$ minutes before $8$:$00$ — the hour showing is still $7$.

steps.title: Past or to?
steps.intro: Up to the 6, say PAST; after it, say TO the next hour.

problems.prompt: A clock shows $2$:$15$. In words that is:
problems.explanation: $15$ minutes is a quarter of the lap ($60 \div 4 = 15$), and the hand is on its way PAST $2$ — quarter past $2$. Quarter to $2$ would be $1$:$45$.

problems.prompt: "Quarter to $10$" in digits is:
problems.explanation: Quarter to $10$ sits $15$ minutes before $10$:$00$, so the hour digit is still $9$: $9$:$45$, since $45 + 15 = 60$ ✓. Writing $10$:$45$ jumps a whole hour ahead.

problems.prompt: From quarter past $5$ to half past $5$ is:
problems.explanation: From the $15$-minute flag to the $30$-minute flag: $15 + 15 = 30$ — one more quarter lap, $15$ minutes.

steps.title: The name looks ahead
steps.prompt: A clock shows $7$:$45$. In words that is:
steps.explanation: $45$ minutes past means three quarter-laps done ($3 \times 15 = 45$) and one to go ($45 + 15 = 60$) — so the name looks ahead: quarter to $8$. "Quarter to $7$" reads the digit instead of the direction.

steps.title: What you learned
points: One hour trades for 60 minutes — never 100.
Minute hand at 12: o'clock, 0 minutes past.
Minute hand at 3: quarter past, 15 minutes (60 divided by 4).
Minute hand at 6: half past, 30 minutes (60 divided by 2).
Minute hand at 9: quarter to the NEXT hour, 45 minutes past this one.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For each clock below, find the MINUTE hand first and say its flag — o'clock, quarter past, half past, or quarter to — then let the hour hand fill in the hour.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: All four flags of the 60-minute lap.

problems.prompt: The minute hand points at $9$. Minutes past the hour:
problems.explanation: The $9$ is the three-quarter flag: $3 \times 15 = 45$ minutes past. Reading the $9$ itself as minutes is the trap.

problems.prompt: $5$:$30$ in words is:
problems.explanation: $30$ minutes is half the lap ($60 \div 2 = 30$): half past $5$. Half past $6$ would show $6$:$30$.

problems.prompt: How many quarter-hours fit in one hour?
problems.explanation: Four quarters rebuild the lap: $4 \times 15 = 60$ minutes.

problems.prompt: From quarter to $9$ until $9$ o'clock is:
problems.explanation: Quarter to means one quarter remains: $45 + 15 = 60$ — just $15$ minutes to the hour.

problems.prompt: The hour hand sits halfway between $10$ and $11$, the minute hand at $6$. The time is:
problems.explanation: Minute hand at $6$: $60 \div 2 = 30$ minutes past. The hour hand halfway between $10$ and $11$ says the hour $10$ is half spent: half past $10$.

steps.title: You've finished "Reading the Clock"
steps.body: The 60-trade and its four flags — o'clock, quarter past, half past, quarter to. Next: the clock in motion — days, weeks, months, and how long things LAST, counted in minutes.

lessons.title: Calendar & Duration
lessons.concreteComparison: A herder's summer runs on two clocks at once. The big one is the calendar: $7$ days to the week, $12$ months to the year, $365$ days in all. The small one is the day itself, where a milking that starts at $8$:$00$ and takes $40$ minutes ends at $8$:$40$ — start plus length gives the end, every single time.
lessons.objective: Use the calendar trades — $7$ days a week, $12$ months and $365$ days a year — and find durations inside one day: start time plus length gives the end time, counted up through the round hour in minutes.
concept: **The week trades for 7 days.** Three weeks are $3 \times 7 = 21$ days; and $30$ days make $4$ full weeks with $2$ days over, since $4 \times 7 + 2 = 30$.

**The year holds 12 months and 365 days.** Months are uneven — $30$ or $31$ days, and February with $28$ — but the year's totals are fixed: $12$ months, $365$ days ($366$ in a leap year, one extra: $365 + 1 = 366$).

**Start + length = end.** A lesson starting at $8$:$00$ and lasting $40$ minutes ends at $8$:$40$. When the minutes would pass the hour, count UP THROUGH the round hour: from $9$:$40$, first $20$ minutes to $10$:$00$, then the rest.
lessons.keyIdea: Weeks trade for 7 days and years for 12 months and 365 days. Inside one day, start plus length equals end — and the round hour is the stepping stone when minutes spill over.

facts.title: The calendar trades
facts.explanation: The week's trade is fixed at 7; the year holds 12 months and 365 days (366 when leap).

facts.title: Start + length = end
facts.explanation: In minutes: 8:00 is 480 minutes into the day, plus a 40-minute lesson lands on 520 — which is 8:40.

workedExamples.statement: Summer camp lasts $3$ weeks. How many days is that?
workedExamples.solution: $3 \times 7 = 21$ days. Three rows of a calendar page — three Mondays, three Sundays, twenty-one boxes.

workedExamples.statement: A maths lesson starts at $8$:$00$ and lasts $40$ minutes. When does it end?
workedExamples.note: Work in minutes: start + length = end.
workedExamples.solution: In minutes since midnight, $8$:$00$ is $8 \times 60 = 480$. Add the length: $480 + 40 = 520$ minutes, which is $8$:$40$ — still inside the same hour, no spill-over.

commonMistakes.correction: Months are uneven: some have 31, some 30, and February has 28 (29 in a leap year). Only the year's totals are fixed — 12 months, 365 days.

commonMistakes.text: Adding minutes straight past the hour — 9:40 plus 30 minutes becomes 9:70.
commonMistakes.correction: There is no 9:70; the hour holds only 60 minutes. Count up through the round hour: 20 minutes reach 10:00, and the other 10 land on 10:10.

tryIt.statement: How many days are in $4$ weeks?
tryIt.solution: $4 \times 7 = 28$ days — exactly February's count in an ordinary year.

tryIt.statement: A film starts at $2$:$00$ and ends at $3$:$30$. How long is it?
tryIt.solution: In minutes: $2$:$00$ is $2 \times 60 = 120$ and $3$:$30$ is $3 \times 60 + 30 = 210$. The length is $90$ minutes, since $120 + 90 = 210$ ✓ — one hour and thirty minutes, as $60 + 30 = 90$.

steps.title: The calendar's trades
beats: The calendar below shows $4$ weeks of $7$ days — $4 \times 7 = 28$ days, which is exactly February in an ordinary year.
The week's trade never bends: $7$ days, always. But months are uneven — $30$ or $31$ days, February $28$ — so a month is ABOUT four weeks, never exactly.
The year's totals are fixed: $12$ months, $365$ days. A leap year adds one: $365 + 1 = 366$.

steps.title: Weeks into days
steps.intro: Multiply by 7 for days; divide by 7 for weeks — remainders welcome.

examples.prompt: How many days in $5$ weeks?
February has $28$ days. How many full weeks is that?
steps: $28 \div 7 = 4$ — exactly four weeks, nothing left over.
Receipt: $4 \times 7 = 28$ ✓. February is the only month that can be all whole weeks.

steps.title: Calendar counts
steps.intro: Say the week's trade — seven — before multiplying.

problems.prompt: $2$ weeks is how many days?
problems.explanation: $2 \times 7 = 14$ days. $9$ adds the $2$ and the $7$ instead of trading.

problems.prompt: How many full weeks fit in $28$ days?
problems.explanation: $28 \div 7 = 4$ weeks, receipt $4 \times 7 = 28$ ✓.

problems.prompt: June has $30$ days. As weeks and days that is:
problems.explanation: $4 \times 7 = 28$, and $2$ more reach $30$: receipt $4 \times 7 + 2 = 30$ with $2 < 7$ ✓. "$3$ weeks $9$ days" hides a whole extra week inside the $9$.

steps.title: The year's totals
steps.prompt: How many days are in an ordinary year, and in a leap year?
steps.explanation: An ordinary year has $365$ days; a leap year adds one extra day at the end of February: $365 + 1 = 366$. The months are uneven, but these totals never change.

steps.title: Why leap years exist
steps.body: A year is $365$ days because that is how long Earth takes to travel once around the Sun — almost. The true trip takes about a quarter of a day longer, so every fourth year the calendar collects the four quarters into one whole extra day: $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$, and February gets a $29$th day.

steps.title: Durations inside one day
beats: How long something lasts obeys one equation: START + LENGTH = END. The timeline below shows it in minutes: $8$:$00$ is $8 \times 60 = 480$ minutes into the day, and a $40$-minute lesson lands on $480 + 40 = 520$ — that is $8$:$40$.
When minutes would spill past the hour, use the round hour as a stepping stone. From $9$:$40$ to $10$:$10$: first $20$ minutes climb to $10$:$00$, then $10$ more — $20 + 10 = 30$ minutes in all.

The spill-over trap has a name: there is no $9$:$70$. The hour holds only $60$ minutes, so every count must STEP ON the round hour, never run straight past it — that is why $9$:$40$ plus $30$ minutes is $10$:$10$, not $9$:$70$.

steps.title: Start, length, end
steps.intro: All three in minutes; the round hour is the stepping stone.

examples.prompt: A lesson starts at $8$:$00$ and lasts $40$ minutes. End time?
How long is it from $9$:$40$ to $10$:$10$?
steps: Step to the round hour: $20$ minutes reach $10$:$00$; then $10$ more.
$20 + 10 = 30$ minutes. Receipt in minutes: $9$:$40$ is $9 \times 60 + 40 = 580$, and $580 + 30 = 610$, which is $10$:$10$ ✓.

steps.title: Count the minutes
steps.intro: Start + length = end — receipt every answer.

problems.prompt: A cartoon starts at $5$:$00$ and lasts $30$ minutes. It ends at:
problems.explanation: $5$:$00$ is $5 \times 60 = 300$ minutes; $300 + 30 = 330$, which is $5$:$30$. Writing $5$:$03$ drops a zero, and $6$:$30$ adds a whole extra hour.
Same hour, so the minutes tell all: from $15$ past to $45$ past is $30$, since $15 + 30 = 45$ ✓.

problems.prompt: Buses leave at $7$:$00$, $7$:$30$ and $8$:$00$. They run every:
problems.explanation: $7$:$00$ is $7 \times 60 = 420$ minutes and $7$:$30$ is $450$: the gap is $30$, since $420 + 30 = 450$ ✓ — and $30$ more reaches $8$:$00$ at $480$.

steps.title: Through the round hour
steps.prompt: Wrestling is on TV from $6$:$30$ to $7$:$15$. How long is that?
steps.explanation: Step through $7$:$00$: from $6$:$30$ that is $30$ minutes, then $15$ more — $30 + 15 = 45$ minutes. Receipt: $6$:$30$ is $6 \times 60 + 30 = 390$ minutes, and $390 + 45 = 435$, which is $7$:$15$ ✓.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The week trades for 7 days — always.
A year holds 12 months and 365 days; a leap year has 366.
Months are uneven: 30 or 31 days, and February with 28.
Start + length = end, with everything counted in minutes.
When minutes spill past the hour, step through the round hour — no 9:70 exists.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every duration below, write start + length = end in minutes and check the sum — the receipt catches every spill-over mistake.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Calendar trades and one-day durations together.

problems.prompt: $6$ weeks is how many days?
problems.explanation: $6 \times 7 = 42$ days. $13$ adds instead of trading.

problems.prompt: A $31$-day month is how many weeks and days?
problems.explanation: $4 \times 7 = 28$, and $3$ more reach $31$: receipt $4 \times 7 + 3 = 31$ with $3 < 7$ ✓.
Climb to the round hour: $20 + 40 = 60$, so $40$ minutes. Receipt: $3$:$20$ is $3 \times 60 + 20 = 200$ minutes and $200 + 40 = 240$, which is $4$:$00$ ✓.

problems.prompt: Football practice starts at $5$:$20$ and lasts $50$ minutes. It ends at:
problems.explanation: $5$:$20$ is $5 \times 60 + 20 = 320$ minutes; $320 + 50 = 370$, which is $6 \times 60 + 10$ — so $6$:$10$. "$5$:$70$" is the spill-over trap: no hour holds $70$ minutes.

problems.prompt: How many days does a leap year have?
problems.explanation: The ordinary $365$ plus February's extra day: $365 + 1 = 366$.

steps.title: You've finished "Calendar & Duration"
steps.body: Weeks of seven, years of twelve months and $365$ days, and the one-day equation start + length = end. Next: the trade you can hold in your hand — togrog notes, and change counted UP instead of down.

lessons.title: Counting Money
lessons.concreteComparison: At the Naadam fair a khuushuur costs $700$ togrog and you hand over a $1\,000$ note. The seller does not subtract — she counts UP, pressing coins into your hand: eight hundred, nine hundred, one thousand. You walk away with $300$ togrog of change, and the receipt is built into the counting: change plus price makes exactly what you paid.
lessons.objective: Total a handful of $500$, $1\,000$, $5\,000$ and $10\,000$ togrog notes, make one amount in different ways, and give change from a round payment by counting up from the price.
concept: **Count value, not paper.** A purse's worth is each note's value times its count, added up: one $5\,000$ note, two $1\,000$ notes and a $500$ note make $5\,000 + 2\,000 + 500 = 7\,500$ togrog. Three notes can beat ten — value decides, never the count of papers.

**Notes trade like units.** Two $500$ notes trade for one $1\,000$ note ($2 \times 500 = 1\,000$); five $1\,000$ notes trade for one $5\,000$. So one amount can be MADE many ways — $4\,000$ is four $1\,000$ notes, or eight $500$ notes.

**Change counts UP.** Price $700$, paid $1\,000$: start at the price and climb to the payment — $800$, $900$, $1\,000$ — that climb is the change, $300$. The receipt is automatic: $300 + 700 = 1\,000$.
lessons.keyIdea: Money is measured in value, not in pieces of paper: total the values, trade notes like units, and give change by counting up from the price to the payment — change plus price equals paid.

facts.title: Notes trade like units
facts.explanation: Two 500-togrog notes are worth one 1000 note; five 1000 notes are worth one 5000 note.

facts.title: Change counts up
facts.explanation: Change plus price equals what was paid — counting up builds the receipt as you go.

workedExamples.statement: A purse holds one $5\,000$ note, two $1\,000$ notes and one $500$ note. How many togrog in all?
workedExamples.note: Value times count for each kind, then add.
workedExamples.solution: $5\,000 + 2 \times 1\,000 + 500 = 5\,000 + 2\,000 + 500 = 7\,500$ togrog. Four pieces of paper, seven and a half thousand of value.

workedExamples.statement: A khuushuur costs $700$ togrog and you pay with a $1\,000$ note. What is your change?
workedExamples.note: Count up from the price to the payment.
workedExamples.solution: Climb from $700$: $800$, $900$, $1\,000$ — three steps of $100$, so the change is $300$ togrog. Receipt: $300 + 700 = 1\,000$ ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Judging a purse by its number of notes — three 1000 notes must beat one 5000 note.
commonMistakes.correction: Count VALUE, not paper: three thousands make 3000, and 3000 < 5000. One big note outweighs a small stack.

commonMistakes.text: Giving change without a receipt, so a slip of 100 goes unnoticed.
commonMistakes.correction: Always add the change back to the price: if change + price does not equal what was paid, the change is wrong. 300 + 700 = 1000 is the whole proof.

tryIt.statement: Show two different ways to make $3\,000$ togrog with notes.
tryIt.solution: Three $1\,000$ notes: $3 \times 1\,000 = 3\,000$. Or six $500$ notes: $6 \times 500 = 3\,000$. Same value, different paper.

tryIt.statement: A book costs $4\,200$ togrog and you pay with a $5\,000$ note. Find the change by counting up.

steps.title: Count value, not paper
beats: Togrog notes come in sizes: $500$, $1\,000$, $5\,000$, $10\,000$. A purse's worth is VALUE times COUNT for each size, added up — the purse below holds $5\,000 + 2\,000 + 500 = 7\,500$ togrog in just four notes.
Notes trade like every unit in this topic: two $500$ notes make a $1\,000$ ($2 \times 500 = 1\,000$), five $1\,000$ notes make a $5\,000$, two $5\,000$ notes make a $10\,000$.
Because of the trades, one amount wears many outfits: $4\,000$ togrog is four $1\,000$ notes, or eight $500$ notes — the value never notices the difference.

steps.title: Purse totals
steps.intro: Biggest notes first; value times count; add.

examples.prompt: Total one $5\,000$ note, two $1\,000$ notes and one $500$ note.
Make $4\,000$ togrog two different ways.
steps: Or eight $500$ notes: $8 \times 500 = 4\,000$ — same value, twice the paper.

steps.title: Total the notes
steps.intro: Value times count — paper is just a costume.

problems.prompt: Two $1\,000$ notes and one $500$ note make:
problems.explanation: $2 \times 1\,000 = 2\,000$, plus $500$: $2\,500$ togrog. $1\,500$ counts only one of the thousands.

problems.prompt: One $5\,000$ note and three $1\,000$ notes make:
problems.explanation: $5\,000 + 3 \times 1\,000 = 5\,000 + 3\,000 = 8\,000$ togrog. $5\,300$ treats the three thousands as three hundreds.

problems.prompt: How many $500$ notes make $2\,000$ togrog?
problems.explanation: $4 \times 500 = 2\,000$ — every pair of $500$s trades for a $1\,000$, and two pairs make two thousand.

steps.title: Paper against value
steps.prompt: Which purse holds more: three $1\,000$ notes, or one $5\,000$ note?
steps.explanation: Count value, not paper: $3 \times 1\,000 = 3\,000$, and $3\,000 < 5\,000$. The single note wins by $2\,000$ togrog ($3\,000 + 2\,000 = 5\,000$ ✓).

steps.title: Shopkeepers count up, not down
steps.body: Watch a market seller give change: she starts at the PRICE and counts upward, laying money in your palm until she reaches what you paid. No subtraction sum in sight — yet it cannot go wrong, because the pile in your hand plus the price adds up to your note. Counting up carries its own receipt.

steps.title: Change by counting up
beats: Change is the climb from the price to what you paid. Price $700$, paid $1\,000$: the line below climbs $800$, $900$, $1\,000$ — three steps of $100$, so the change is $300$ togrog.
The receipt comes free: CHANGE + PRICE = PAID, here $300 + 700 = 1\,000$ ✓. If the sum misses, the change is wrong — no exceptions.
Bigger gaps use bigger steps: price $3\,200$, paid $5\,000$ — up $800$ to $4\,000$, then $1\,000$ more: change $1\,800$, and $1\,800 + 3\,200 = 5\,000$ ✓.

steps.title: The counting-up till
steps.intro: Climb from price to payment; the climb IS the change.

examples.prompt: Price $700$ togrog, paid with a $1\,000$ note. Change?
Price $3\,200$ togrog, paid with a $5\,000$ note. Change?

steps.title: Climb to the note
steps.intro: Count up, then receipt: change + price = paid.

problems.prompt: Sweets cost $600$ togrog; you pay with a $1\,000$ note. Change:
problems.explanation: Climb from $600$ to $1\,000$: four hundreds. Receipt: $400 + 600 = 1\,000$ ✓. Answering $600$ hands back the price itself.

problems.prompt: A notebook costs $1\,500$ togrog; you pay $2\,000$. Change:
A toy costs $7\,300$ togrog; you pay with a $10\,000$ note. Change:

steps.title: Receipt the change
steps.prompt: A bowl of airag costs $900$ togrog; you pay with a $1\,000$ note. Your change is:
steps.explanation: One small step: from $900$ to $1\,000$ is $100$. Receipt: $100 + 900 = 1\,000$ ✓ — any other answer fails the add-back.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Purse totals: each note's value times its count, added up — value beats paper.
Notes trade like units: two 500s make a 1000, five 1000s make a 5000.
One amount can be made many ways with different notes.
Change counts UP from the price to the payment.
The receipt is law: change + price = paid, every time.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every change question below, count up first, then say the receipt out loud — change plus price equals paid. If the receipt fails, climb again.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Totals, trades, and change with receipts.

problems.prompt: One $5\,000$ note, four $1\,000$ notes and one $500$ note make:
problems.explanation: $5\,000 + 4 \times 1\,000 + 500 = 5\,000 + 4\,000 + 500 = 9\,500$ togrog. The $9\,050$ trap wrote the $500$ in the tens column instead of the hundreds.

problems.prompt: How many $1\,000$ notes make $10\,000$ togrog?
problems.explanation: $10 \times 1\,000 = 10\,000$ — or two $5\,000$ notes, since $2 \times 5\,000 = 10\,000$ says the same value in less paper.

problems.prompt: A pencil costs $450$ togrog; you pay with a $500$ note. Change:
problems.explanation: A short climb: from $450$ to $500$ is $50$. Receipt: $50 + 450 = 500$ ✓.

problems.prompt: A khuushuur costs $800$ togrog and tea costs $400$. You pay for both with a $2\,000$ note. Change:
A book costs $4\,500$ togrog and a toy costs $5\,000$. The toy costs more by:

steps.title: You've finished "Counting Money" — and the topic
steps.body: Rulers, scales, jugs, clocks, calendars and purses — six faces of one idea: KNOW THE TRADE, then count. $100$ centimetres to the metre, $1\,000$ grams to the kilogram, $60$ minutes to the hour, $7$ days to the week, and two $500$ notes to the thousand. Every measurement you will ever make starts with a trade like these.

practice.statement: Convert $8$ m to centimetres, and say which is longer: $8$ m or $750$ cm.
practice.solution: Trade: $8 \times 100 = 800$ cm. Then $800 > 750$ — the $8$ m is longer by $50$ cm, since $750 + 50 = 800$ ✓.

practice.statement: A pencil lies along a ruler from the $3$ cm mark to the $11$ cm mark. How long is the pencil?
practice.solution: Mark to mark: $11 - 3 = 8$ cm. Add back: $8 + 3 = 11$ ✓.

practice.statement: Convert $7$ kg to grams, and $2\,000$ g to kilograms.
practice.solution: Big to small: $7 \times 1\,000 = 7\,000$ g. Small to big: $2\,000 \div 1\,000 = 2$ kg, receipt $2 \times 1\,000 = 2\,000$ ✓.

practice.statement: Which holds more: a pot of $1$ l $300$ ml, or a bottle of $1\,250$ ml?
Write "quarter to $6$" in digits, and say where the minute hand points.
practice.solution: Quarter to $6$ is $15$ minutes before $6$:$00$, so the hour showing is $5$ with $3 \times 15 = 45$ minutes past: $5$:$45$, minute hand at the $9$. Check: $45 + 15 = 60$ ✓.

practice.statement: A pony trek lasts $3$ weeks and $4$ days. How many days is that in all?
practice.solution: Trade the weeks: $3 \times 7 = 21$ days, plus the $4$ loose days: $21 + 4 = 25$ days. Receipt: $3 \times 7 + 4 = 25$ with $4 < 7$ ✓.

practice.statement: Choir practice runs from $4$:$50$ to $5$:$30$. How long is it?
practice.solution: Step through the round hour: $10$ minutes reach $5$:$00$, then $30$ more — $10 + 30 = 40$ minutes. Receipt in minutes: $4$:$50$ is $4 \times 60 + 50 = 290$, and $290 + 40 = 330$, which is $5$:$30$ ✓.

practice.statement: A deel costs $6\,400$ togrog and you pay with a $10\,000$ note. Find the change by counting up.

testYourself.statement: Convert $600$ cm to metres and $4$ m to centimetres. Then say which is longer: $4$ m or $380$ cm.
testYourself.solution: $600 \div 100 = 6$ m (receipt $6 \times 100 = 600$ ✓) and $4 \times 100 = 400$ cm. Comparing: $380 < 400$, so the $4$ m is longer.

testYourself.statement: Which is heavier: $3$ kg or $2\,800$ g? Which holds more: $2$ l or $2\,200$ ml?
testYourself.solution: Mass: $3$ kg $= 3\,000$ g and $2\,800 < 3\,000$ — the $3$ kg wins. Capacity: $2$ l $= 2\,000$ ml and $2\,200 > 2\,000$ — the $2\,200$ ml wins. Trade first, compare second, both times.

testYourself.statement: The minute hand points at $9$ and the hour hand sits just before $8$. What time is it, in words and in digits?
testYourself.solution: Minute hand at $9$: three quarter-laps done, $3 \times 15 = 45$ minutes past. The hour hand has nearly finished hour $7$: the time is $7$:$45$ — quarter to $8$, since $45 + 15 = 60$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: How many days are in a leap year? And how many full weeks are in $35$ days?
testYourself.solution: A leap year adds one day to $365$: $365 + 1 = 366$ days. Weeks: $35 \div 7 = 5$, receipt $5 \times 7 = 35$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: A concert starts at $7$:$15$ and lasts $45$ minutes. When does it end?
testYourself.solution: In minutes: $7$:$15$ is $7 \times 60 + 15 = 435$. Add the length: $435 + 45 = 480$, which is $8 \times 60$ — exactly $8$:$00$. The quarters agree: $15 + 45 = 60$, one whole hour's worth of minutes closed.

testYourself.statement: Fabric for a deel costs $7\,500$ togrog and you pay with a $10\,000$ note. Find the change by counting up, and say which notes the seller could hand you.
testYourself.solution: Climb: $500$ reaches $8\,000$, then $2\,000$ more reaches $10\,000$ — change $500 + 2\,000 = 2\,500$ togrog. Receipt: $2\,500 + 7\,500 = 10\,000$ ✓. The seller could hand you two $1\,000$ notes and one $500$ note: $2 \times 1\,000 + 500 = 2\,500$ ✓.
